question: You need to nest a parenthetical inside another parenthetical: '(the plan ___ which was long ___ worked).' Under Chicago style, which brackets go in the inner position?
answer: Square brackets: '(the plan [which was long] worked)'
choices: Square brackets: '(the plan [which was long] worked)'
More round parentheses: '(the plan ((which was long)) worked)'
Curly braces: '(the plan {which was long} worked)'
Angle brackets: '(the plan <which was long> worked)'
context: Chicago uses square brackets for the inner nesting to make the two levels visually distinct. Some editors instead use double parens; Chicago does not. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.101.

question: An article quotes Lincoln: 'shall not perish from the earth.' To make the pronoun clear, an editor inserts 'the government' at the start. How should the insertion be marked?
answer: In square brackets: 'Lincoln wrote that "[the government] shall not perish from the earth."'
choices: In square brackets: 'Lincoln wrote that "[the government] shall not perish from the earth."'
In round parentheses: 'Lincoln wrote that "(the government) shall not perish from the earth."'
In italics with no brackets: 'Lincoln wrote that "the government shall not perish from the earth."'
In ALL CAPS: 'Lincoln wrote that "THE GOVERNMENT shall not perish from the earth."'
context: Anything the editor adds to a quotation goes in square brackets so the reader can tell what came from the original and what was added for clarity. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 13.59.

question: A grocer's sign says 'APPLE'S 1 POUND.' An article quotes this sign and wants to preserve the misspelled apostrophe but signal that the error is in the original. What mark is inserted, and where?
answer: [sic] after the misspelled word: 'The sign read "apple's [sic] 1 pound."'
choices: [sic] after the misspelled word: 'The sign read "apple's [sic] 1 pound."'
No mark -- always silently correct quoted errors
context: [sic] is Latin for 'thus, so' -- an editor's polite way to say 'we know it looks wrong; that is what the original wrote.' Source: MLA Handbook on [sic].

question: Compare '"I was going to..."' (author's trailing-off ellipsis) with '"the general marched [...] to the river"' (a shortened quotation). What is the difference the brackets around the ellipsis signal?
answer: Plain '...' is the AUTHOR'S trailing-off; '[...]' is an EDITOR'S deleted words INSIDE a quotation
choices: Plain '...' is the AUTHOR'S trailing-off; '[...]' is an EDITOR'S deleted words INSIDE a quotation
Both are the same; brackets are optional
Plain '...' is an editor's cut; '[...]' is an author's trailing-off
Plain '...' is used in fiction; '[...]' is used in nonfiction
context: Bracketed ellipsis tells the reader 'the editor removed some words from the original text here.' Plain ellipsis is part of the quoted author's own text. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 13.58.

question: In which sentence does the writer correctly use BRACKETS for an editorial insertion?
answer: 'The witness said, "He [the suspect] arrived at midnight."'
choices: 'The witness said, "He [the suspect] arrived at midnight."'
'The witness said, "He (the suspect) arrived at midnight."'
'The witness said, "He, the suspect, arrived at midnight."'
'The witness said, "He {the suspect} arrived at midnight."'
context: The clarifying phrase THE SUSPECT was added by the writer INTO the witness's quoted words. Square brackets mark it as an editorial insertion. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 13.59.

question: 'Mistakes were made.' Why is this the classic example of passive voice hiding an actor?
answer: the sentence names the mistake but not the person who made it
choices: the sentence names the mistake but not the person who made it
context: PASSIVE VOICE can hide the actor. 'Mistakes were made' names the fact of the mistake without naming who made it. Active version: 'I made mistakes.' The active version assigns responsibility.

question: What is PASSIVE VOICE grammatically?
answer: a sentence where the SUBJECT receives the action (formed with 'to be' + past participle)
choices: a sentence where the SUBJECT receives the action (formed with 'to be' + past participle)
context: PASSIVE = subject receives the action. Formed with 'to be' + past participle: 'The ball WAS THROWN by Tom.' Compare ACTIVE: 'Tom threw the ball' (subject does the action).

question: When IS passive voice appropriate?
answer: when the actor is unknown, obvious, or unimportant to the point (e.g. 'my bike was stolen')
choices: when the actor is unknown, obvious, or unimportant to the point (e.g. 'my bike was stolen')
context: PASSIVE is CORRECT when: actor unknown ('my bike was stolen'), obvious ('the suspect was arrested'), or unimportant ('water is boiled at 100 degrees'). Scientific writing uses passive to focus on process.

question: 'The vase was broken.' vs 'The cat knocked the vase off the shelf.' Which sentence tells more of a story?
answer: the second (active, names the actor and the action)
choices: the second (active, names the actor and the action)
context: ACTIVE VOICE assigns responsibility and tells a story. Passive can hide who did what. When the actor matters, name them. When the actor doesn't matter, passive is fine.

question: 'Errors were discovered in the report.' If the auditor found them, active would be ___.
answer: 'The auditor found errors in the report.'
choices: 'The auditor found errors in the report.'
context: ACTIVE VOICE puts the actor first (the auditor) and describes what they did (found). The passive version drops the auditor entirely, hiding who caught the errors.

question: 'Water is boiled at 100 degrees Celsius.' Why is passive appropriate here?
answer: the actor (whoever is doing the boiling) is unimportant; the physical process is the point
choices: the actor (whoever is doing the boiling) is unimportant; the physical process is the point
scientific writing does not allow passive
context: SCIENTIFIC WRITING often uses passive to focus on the PHENOMENON, not the researcher. 'Water is boiled' emphasises the physical fact; who did the boiling doesn't matter to the science.

question: Which sentence uses passive voice to HIDE responsibility that should be assigned?
answer: 'Company funds were misused' (by whom?)
choices: 'The results were verified by three labs'
context: The first sentence hides who misused the funds -- classic responsibility-hiding passive. The others have known agents (police), obvious contexts (historical event), or explicit agents (three labs).

question: 'The report was completed on Friday' -- is this an acceptable passive?
answer: depends: OK if the writer isn't important; problematic if the reader needs to know who wrote it
choices: depends: OK if the writer isn't important; problematic if the reader needs to know who wrote it
context: CONTEXT-DEPENDENT: 'The report was completed on Friday' is fine as a status update. 'The manager's report was completed' hides who did the work. Ask: does the reader need to know the actor?

question: Which sentence uses PASSIVE voice?
answer: The ball was thrown across the field.
choices: The ball was thrown across the field.
The ball flew across the field.
Tom threw the ball across the field.
The ball is in the field.
context: 'Was thrown' = 'to be' + past participle = PASSIVE. Subject 'the ball' receives the action. The other options use active verbs (flew, threw) or a linking verb (is).

question: An online review: "That story really peaked my interest." Which word was misused?
answer: "peaked" (should be "piqued")
context: PIQUED = aroused/provoked. Interest is stirred up, not reaching a summit. Most-corrected misuse online.

question: "She peeked through the curtains." What does PEEKED mean?
answer: took a quick look
context: PEEKED = brief glance, often secretly. Two Es like two EYES peeking.

question: Memory tricks for PEAK / PEEK / PIQUE?
answer: PEAK has a peak (triangle-A); PEEK has two EEs like two eyes; PIQUE = French for sharp point
choices: PEAK has a peak (triangle-A); PEEK has two EEs like two eyes; PIQUE = French for sharp point
PEAK is British; PEEK is American; PIQUE is Latin
all three come from the same Greek root
PEAK is a noun only; PEEK is a verb only; PIQUE is an adjective only
context: Each spelling contains a visual clue to its meaning: mountain-A, twin eyes, or sharp Q.

question: "The mountain ___ at 14,000 feet." Which verb fits?
answer: peaked
context: PEAKED = reached the highest point. Mountains reach a summit.

question: Which sentence uses PIQUED correctly?
answer: The mystery novel piqued her curiosity from page one
choices: The mystery novel piqued her curiosity from page one
The climber piqued the summit at dawn
The child piqued through the keyhole
context: PIQUED = stirred up, aroused. Curiosity is stirred, not reached. The other three want PEAKED or PEEKED.

question: The correct phrase for arousing interest is always "___ my interest." Which word fills it?
answer: piqued
context: PIQUED my interest = stirred up my interest. The internet's most-corrected homophone misuse.

question: PIQUE entered English in the 1600s from French. What is the older idiom still in use?
answer: a fit of pique (a moment of resentment)
choices: a fit of pique (a moment of resentment)
a peak of pique (a burst of energy)
a peek of pique (a brief glimpse)
a pique of interest (a low ebb)
context: A FIT OF PIQUE = a moment of irritation or resentment. Original French sense. Modern "piqued interest" grew from "sharply provoke."

question: In Lewis Carroll's 'Through the Looking-Glass' (1871), Humpty Dumpty tells Alice a certain kind of word is 'like a suitcase with two hinged compartments -- two meanings packed up into one word.' What is the name for that kind of blended word?
answer: A portmanteau
context: PORTMANTEAU was an old-fashioned travel case that opened into two hinged halves -- Carroll's perfect image for a word packing two meanings. Source: Lewis Carroll, 'Through the Looking-Glass' (1871) Chapter VI.

question: The word BRUNCH is a portmanteau blending two source words. Which two?
answer: Breakfast + lunch
context: Same trick with SMOG (smoke + fog), MOTEL (motor + hotel), SPORK (spoon + fork). Source: Grokipedia 'Portmanteau' (2026-09-05).

question: The word PODCAST is a portmanteau of which two source words?
answer: iPod + broadcast
context: PODCAST was coined in the early 2000s as personal audio broadcasts to iPods. Same era: EMOTICON (emotion + icon), SITCOM (situation + comedy), INFOMERCIAL (information + commercial). Source: Grokipedia 'Portmanteau' (2026-09-05).

question: Lewis Carroll made up dozens of portmanteau words for his poem 'Jabberwocky' (1871). Two of them actually escaped the poem and became ordinary English words. Which two?
answer: CHORTLE (chuckle + snort) and GALUMPHING (gallop + triumphing)
context: The Oxford English Dictionary lists both CHORTLE and GALUMPHING as first attested in 1871 in Carroll. SLITHY and MIMSY appear in the poem but never became common English. Source: OED entries.

question: A portmanteau BLENDS two words, sharing sounds where they meet (SMOG = smoke + fog). A COMPOUND WORD sticks two words together with both intact (bookshelf). An ACRONYM uses initials of a phrase (NASA). Which of these is a PORTMANTEAU?
answer: SPORK (spoon + fork)
context: SPORK blends SPOON and FORK, sharing letters (SP-O-RK). SUNFLOWER and BOOKSHELF are compounds (both source words fully intact). SCUBA is an acronym. Source: Grokipedia 'Portmanteau' (2026-09-05).

question: Which of these words is an ACRONYM (initials of a phrase) rather than a portmanteau or compound?
answer: NASA -- National Aeronautics and Space Administration
choices: NASA -- National Aeronautics and Space Administration
context: NASA takes the first letters of a phrase and pronounces them as a word -- that is an acronym. The others are portmanteaus or compounds. Source: Grokipedia 'Acronym' (2026-09-05).

question: 'The dog's bone was buried.' Where does the apostrophe go for a singular possessive?
answer: before the s (dog's)
context: Singular noun + apostrophe + s = possessive. 'The dog's bone' = the bone belonging to the (one) dog. Chicago 7.16.

question: 'The dogs' bones were in a pile.' Where is the apostrophe for a PLURAL possessive?
answer: after the s (dogs')
context: Plural noun already ending in s + apostrophe (no extra s) = plural possessive. 'The dogs' bones' = the bones belonging to more than one dog. Chicago 7.17.

question: 'Its the children's toys that are missing.' Which possessive is written correctly?
answer: children's (irregular plural takes apostrophe-s)
context: Irregular plurals that do NOT end in s (children, women, men, mice) take apostrophe-s just like singulars: children's, women's, men's, mice's.

question: 'The Smith's live next door.' What is wrong with this sentence?
answer: should be 'the Smiths' -- plural, not possessive
choices: should be 'the Smiths' -- plural, not possessive
context: The Smiths (plural) live next door. Adding an apostrophe makes it possessive without a noun for them to possess -- a classic apostrophe error found on mailboxes everywhere.

question: 'James's book' or 'James' book' -- which does the Chicago Manual of Style prefer for names ending in s?
answer: James's (add apostrophe-s to singular names, even those ending in s)
choices: James's (add apostrophe-s to singular names, even those ending in s)
context: Chicago 7.17 recommends apostrophe-s for singular names ending in s: James's, Charles's, Jesus's. AP Stylebook is the exception (uses apostrophe only for classical/biblical names). Follow your house style.

question: 'Jesus' teachings' or 'Jesus's teachings' -- when does the AP Stylebook exception apply?
answer: classical and biblical singular names take just the apostrophe (Jesus', Moses', Achilles')
choices: classical and biblical singular names take just the apostrophe (Jesus', Moses', Achilles')
all names ending in s take just the apostrophe
context: AP Stylebook's biblical/classical exception: Jesus', Moses', Achilles', Xerxes'. Chicago disagrees (recommends apostrophe-s for all). This is the one place the two major style guides genuinely split.

question: 'The teachers lounge is on the second floor.' If the lounge belongs to MORE THAN ONE teacher, where does the apostrophe go?
answer: teachers' (plural possessive, apostrophe after the s)
choices: teachers' (plural possessive, apostrophe after the s)
context: The lounge belongs to the teachers (plural) = teachers' lounge. If it were one teacher's lounge, it would be teacher's. Office/school signs constantly get this wrong.

question: 'The PRINCIPAL of the story is: don't lie.' Something is wrong with that sentence. Which correction is right?
answer: Change PRINCIPAL to PRINCIPLE -- a rule of behavior is spelled -ple
choices: Change PRINCIPAL to PRINCIPLE -- a rule of behavior is spelled -ple
Change STORY to TALE -- 'principal' only fits with 'tale'
Change DON'T to DO NOT -- contractions do not fit 'principal'
Leave it -- 'principal' is a synonym for lesson
context: A rule of behavior is a PRINCIPLE. PRINCIPAL means the head of a school, the main thing, or the original loan amount. Source: Merriam-Webster 'principal' + 'principle.'

question: There is a classroom memory trick for keeping the two words straight: your Princip___ is your ___ (a person you know at school). Which pair fills the blanks?
answer: PrincipAL ... PAL
context: PrincipAL ends in -PAL: your PAL. PrinciPLE ends in -PLE: a ruLE. Source: Grokipedia 'Principal vs principle' (2026-09-05).

question: 'The ___ reason our team won was practice, not luck.' Which word fills the blank?
answer: principal -- meaning 'main' or 'most important'
choices: principality -- a small state ruled by a prince
context: Swap test: 'the main reason' works, so PRINCIPAL. PRINCIPLE would only fit if we meant a rule ('a matter of principle'). Source: Merriam-Webster usage note.

question: 'She refused the bribe on a matter of ___.' Which word fills the blank?
answer: principle -- a rule she lives by
choices: principle -- a rule she lives by
context: A matter of RULE or BELIEF -> PRINCIPLE. Swap test: 'a matter of rule' works. Source: Merriam-Webster usage note.

question: When you take out a loan, the bank charges interest on top of the original amount borrowed. What is the finance word for that original amount, before interest is added?
answer: principal -- the main sum of money in a loan
choices: principal -- the main sum of money in a loan
principle -- the rule of interest calculation
prime -- the top interest rate available
context: In finance, PRINCIPAL keeps the 'main' meaning -- the main amount of money the loan started with. Interest is then computed on the principal. Source: Merriam-Webster 'principal' finance sense.

question: 'The ___ of our school teaches us the ___ of honesty at every assembly.' Which pair of words fills the blanks correctly?
answer: principal ... principle
context: The person who leads the school = PRINCIPAL (your pal). The rule she teaches = PRINCIPLE. Two spellings, two jobs. Source: Merriam-Webster 'principal' + 'principle.'

question: 'The ___ argument in the essay is that the ___ of free speech has ancient roots.' Which pair of words fills the blanks correctly?
answer: principal ... principle
context: 'The MAIN argument' -> PRINCIPAL. 'The RULE / belief of free speech' -> PRINCIPLE. Source: Merriam-Webster usage note.

question: 'The team lost ___ first game.' Which possessive pronoun?
answer: its (team is a singular collective in American English)
choices: its (team is a singular collective in American English)
context: PRONOUN-ANTECEDENT AGREEMENT: pronouns must match their antecedent in number. 'The team' (singular collective in US English) → 'its'. UK English often uses 'their'.

question: 'Each student must bring ___ own materials.' Which possessive is now widely accepted?
answer: their (singular THEY, accepted by AP, Chicago, Merriam-Webster)
choices: their (singular THEY, accepted by AP, Chicago, Merriam-Webster)
context: Singular THEIR after singular indefinite pronouns is accepted in modern edited English. The verb ('must bring') stays singular; only the possessive goes plural.

question: 'Neither of the girls remembered ___ book.' Which possessive?
answer: both her and their are widely accepted
choices: her (neither is singular, referring to girls)
both her and their are widely accepted
context: 'Her' matches the singular NEITHER and the gender of 'girls'. 'Their' as singular is also standard. Modern editing accepts both; older editing insists on 'her'.

question: Which sentence has a pronoun-antecedent problem?
answer: The company gave their employees a bonus.
choices: Everyone must bring their notebook, so they can take notes.
The company gave their employees a bonus.
Neither answer is correct because it is missing detail.
Each of the runners set their pace.
context: 'The company' (singular) → 'its employees', not 'their employees'. This is a common error. 'The company gave its employees a bonus' is the fix in American English.

question: 'Everyone raised their hand.' Why is this now grammatically accepted?
answer: singular THEY is accepted for indefinite pronouns; 'their' is gender-neutral and older than 'his' as the default
choices: singular THEY is accepted for indefinite pronouns; 'their' is gender-neutral and older than 'his' as the default
context: Singular THEIR/THEY was used by Chaucer, Shakespeare, and Austen. The 1745 'use HIS as generic' rule was a prescriptive invention. Modern style guides (Chicago 5.48) accept singular THEY.

question: 'The staff completed their reports.' In American English, when is 'their' acceptable with 'staff'?
answer: when emphasising the individual staff members' actions (each writing a report)
choices: when emphasising the individual staff members' actions (each writing a report)
context: Collective nouns permit 'their' when the members act individually. 'The staff their reports' works because each member wrote one. 'The staff its report' would suggest one collective report.

question: 'Anybody can improve if ___ practises.' Which pronoun matches modern gender-neutral style?
answer: they (singular THEY, accepted for indefinite pronouns)
choices: they (singular THEY, accepted for indefinite pronouns)
context: Singular THEY has been the natural gender-neutral English pronoun for centuries. 'Anybody... they' matches modern practice and predates the 18th-century 'generic he' prescription.

question: 'The jury reached ___ verdict.' In careful American English, which possessive is standard?
answer: its (jury as unified body reaching one verdict)
choices: its (jury as unified body reaching one verdict)
either works equally in this context
context: When a collective noun acts as ONE UNIT (reaching one verdict), American English strongly prefers singular 'its'. 'The jury reached their verdicts' would suggest multiple verdicts.

question: In casual texting, ending a single-message text with a period ("ok.") reads as what?
answer: CURT or ANGRY (per linguistic research on iMessage register, McCulloch 2019)
choices: CURT or ANGRY (per linguistic research on iMessage register, McCulloch 2019)
context: Gretchen McCulloch's "Because Internet" (2019) documents this register shift. Same period, opposite reading depending on register.

question: "ok..." (ellipsis in texting) reads as what?
answer: PASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE or HESITANT (per McCulloch)
context: Casual ellipsis in text has taken on tonal meaning. Contrast with the formal ellipsis for omissions in quoted material.

question: What is the ALL-CAPS convention in prose?
answer: SHOUTING; formal writing uses italics for emphasis instead
choices: SHOUTING; formal writing uses italics for emphasis instead
a required style for chapter titles
context: Chicago and AP both regard all-caps in running prose as shouting. Use italics for word-level emphasis in formal writing.

question: What is the current style-guide position on EMOJIS in formal writing?
answer: casual-register only; formal style guides (Chicago 17th ed.) do not have a formal rule and treat emojis as informal
choices: casual-register only; formal style guides (Chicago 17th ed.) do not have a formal rule and treat emojis as informal
context: Style guides have not fully caught up. Chicago punts explicitly. Treat as informal register only.

question: Multiple punctuation for emphasis in text -- "!!!", "???", "ok?????" -- fits which register?
answer: casual text; nonstandard in formal writing (compare the interrobang for incredulous questions)
choices: casual text; nonstandard in formal writing (compare the interrobang for incredulous questions)
academic prose; standard in scholarly writing
context: Strong emotion in casual text uses repeated marks. Formal writing keeps to one mark. The interrobang (?!) is the formal-ish equivalent for incredulous questions.

question: In American usage, titles like Doctor, Mister, Missus abbreviate as Dr., Mr., Mrs. What punctuation follows each of these titles?
answer: A period after the abbreviated title
choices: A period after the abbreviated title
A comma after the abbreviated title
A colon after the abbreviated title
No punctuation follows the abbreviated title
context: American style keeps periods on shortened titles (Dr., Mr., Mrs., Ms.). British style often drops them (Dr, Mr, Mrs, Ms). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 10.4.

question: Under CHICAGO 17th-edition style, which of these degree abbreviations is preferred?
answer: PhD (no periods)
context: Chicago 17e recommends dropping periods from academic-degree abbreviations. Older Chicago and many other style guides retain them (Ph.D., M.D., B.A.). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 10.42.

question: A newspaper prints 'U.S. troops arrived Tuesday.' Which style is being followed?
answer: AP style -- AP keeps the periods in U.S. as noun and adjective
choices: AP style -- AP keeps the periods in U.S. as noun and adjective
Chicago 17e -- Chicago now drops periods (would print 'US troops')
British Fowler's -- Fowler's drops periods (would print 'US troops')
MLA -- MLA never uses country abbreviations
context: AP retains periods on U.S. (though 'US' is fine in AP headlines). Chicago 17e drops them. Both are correct within their house style. Source: AP Stylebook 2020; Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 10.32.

question: The Latin abbreviation e.g. stands for 'exempli gratia' -- 'for example.' In American usage, what punctuation typically follows it in a running sentence?
answer: A comma after the period ('e.g., a cat, a dog')
choices: A comma after the period ('e.g., a cat, a dog')
No punctuation ('e.g. a cat, a dog')
A colon after the period ('e.g.: a cat, a dog')
A semicolon after the period ('e.g.; a cat, a dog')
context: American style follows e.g. and i.e. with a comma. British style often omits the comma. Same for i.e. ('that is') and etc. ('and so forth'). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.51.

question: A sentence ends with the abbreviation U.S.: 'The bill was passed by the U.S.' How many periods should appear at the very end?
answer: One period -- the abbreviation period and the sentence-ending period are the same period
choices: One period -- the abbreviation period and the sentence-ending period are the same period
Two periods -- one for the abbreviation, one for the sentence end
Three periods -- treated as an ellipsis
No period at all -- abbreviations at end need no additional mark
context: The period after 'S' does double duty. Never write 'U.S..' with two periods -- the mark collapses. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 10.5.

question: The same idea can be interrupted three ways: with commas, with em-dashes, or with parentheses. Which choice is the QUIETEST -- the one that pushes the aside most into the background?
answer: Parentheses -- they lower the volume of the aside
choices: Parentheses -- they lower the volume of the aside
Em-dashes -- they turn down the volume
Commas -- they whisper more than the other two
context: Three strengths: commas = mild integrated aside; em-dashes = dramatic emphatic interruption; parentheses = quiet backgrounded aside. Same content; different energy. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.85.

question: A writer wants to make the aside 'which had taken months' as EMPHATIC as possible. Which version of 'The plan ___ which had taken months ___ finally worked' hits hardest?
answer: 'The plan -- which had taken months -- finally worked.' (em-dashes)
choices: 'The plan -- which had taken months -- finally worked.' (em-dashes)
'The plan, which had taken months, finally worked.' (commas)
'The plan (which had taken months) finally worked.' (parentheses)
'The plan: which had taken months: finally worked.' (colons)
context: Em-dashes turn up the volume on a parenthetical. Commas whisper; parentheses back off; em-dashes shout. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.85.

question: A parenthetical is a COMPLETE sentence of its own, in the middle of a paragraph. Where does its ending punctuation go?
answer: Inside the parentheses: '(She was tired.)'
choices: Only after the closing paren, not before: '(She was tired).'
context: A complete-sentence parenthetical takes its own end punctuation INSIDE the parens. Compare with a parenthetical that INTERRUPTS another sentence: 'She was tired (as usual).' where the period stays outside. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.13.

question: '(the plan (which was long) worked)' has parentheses inside parentheses. Under Chicago style, what is the fix?
answer: Use square brackets for the inner: '(the plan [which was long] worked)'
choices: Use square brackets for the inner: '(the plan [which was long] worked)'
Use curly braces for the inner: '(the plan {which was long} worked)'
Leave as-is -- double parens are standard
context: Chicago uses brackets for the inner nesting to keep the two levels visually distinct. Or recast to drop the nesting entirely. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.101.

question: 'Alice, our director, who also, on occasion, sings, will speak.' The sentence has too many commas. Which fix is cleanest?
answer: 'Alice -- our director, who also on occasion sings -- will speak.' (em-dashes bracket the outer aside)
choices: 'Alice -- our director, who also on occasion sings -- will speak.' (em-dashes bracket the outer aside)
'Alice; our director; who also; on occasion; sings; will speak.' (semicolons everywhere)
'Alice: our director: who also: on occasion: sings: will speak.' (colons everywhere)
'Alice (our director, who also, on occasion, sings) will speak.' (parens keep the comma jungle)
context: When commas cluster, promote the outermost pair to em-dashes so the reader can see where the aside starts and ends. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.85.

question: Which of these sentences correctly punctuates a COMPLETE-sentence parenthetical inside a paragraph?
answer: 'The plan finally worked. (It had taken months.) Everyone celebrated.'
choices: 'The plan finally worked. (It had taken months.) Everyone celebrated.'
'The plan finally worked. (It had taken months). Everyone celebrated.'
'The plan finally worked. It had taken months. Everyone celebrated. ()'
'The plan finally worked (It had taken months.) Everyone celebrated.'
context: A stand-alone parenthetical sentence takes its own period INSIDE the parens and starts with a capital letter. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.13.

question: 'Where did you go' is missing something at the end. Which mark should close a direct query like this one?
answer: A question mark (?)
context: Direct questions always end with a question mark. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.42.

question: 'She asked where I went?' Something is wrong here. What is the fix?
answer: Change the question mark to a period -- this is an INDIRECT question (statement about a question, not a question)
choices: Change the question mark to a period -- this is an INDIRECT question (statement about a question, not a question)
Change WHERE to WHERE'S -- to signal a question
Add commas around WHERE I WENT -- appositive apposition
Capitalize WHERE -- questions always take capitals
context: The sentence describes what she asked; it does not ASK the question itself. Indirect questions end with a period. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.42.

question: 'She asked, ___ where did you go?___' The quoted material IS the question. Where does the question mark go?
answer: Inside the closing quotation mark: 'She asked, "Where did you go?"'
choices: Inside the closing quotation mark: 'She asked, "Where did you go?"'
Outside the closing quotation mark: 'She asked, "Where did you go"?'
Before the quotation mark and after: '"?"'
Not needed -- indirect questions never take question marks
context: When the quoted material is the question, the question mark goes INSIDE the closing quotation mark. When the outer sentence is the question about the quoted material, the mark goes outside. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.70.

question: 'You're coming, ___' -- a speaker adds 'aren't you' at the end, turning a statement into a check. What is that construction called, and what mark ends the sentence?
answer: A TAG QUESTION -- ends with a question mark: 'You're coming, aren't you?'
choices: A TAG QUESTION -- ends with a question mark: 'You're coming, aren't you?'
A TAGGED CLAUSE -- ends with a period
A PARTICIPLE PHRASE -- ends with a comma
A NOUN PHRASE -- ends with no punctuation
context: The tag ('aren't you,' 'won't they,' 'have you') turns a statement into a question. End with a question mark. Source: Grokipedia 'Question mark' (2026-09-05).

question: 'Did she ask where you were?' -- a QUESTION about a QUESTION. Under Chicago style, how many question marks should this end with?
answer: One -- the outer question's mark suffices; do not add a second inside for the reported question
choices: One -- the outer question's mark suffices; do not add a second inside for the reported question
Two -- one for each question, stacked
Zero -- both questions cancel each other out
Three -- one for each question plus one for emphasis
context: Chicago uses only ONE question mark here because the inner question is REPORTED (indirect), not quoted directly. If it were quoted -- 'Did she ask, "where are you?"' -- the single inner mark suffices. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.70.

question: In AMERICAN usage, where do periods and commas go relative to closing quotation marks?
answer: Always inside: 'She said "hello."'
choices: Only inside when the punctuation is part of the quote
Only outside when the punctuation is part of the quote
context: American rule: periods and commas ALWAYS go inside, even if not logically part of the quoted material. It is a house-style convention, not a logical rule. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.9.

question: A British newspaper prints 'She said "hello".' with the period OUTSIDE the closing quotation mark. Which style is this?
answer: British -- puts periods and commas OUTSIDE when they are not part of the quote (logical punctuation)
choices: British -- puts periods and commas OUTSIDE when they are not part of the quote (logical punctuation)
Wrong under both British and American rules
context: British style uses LOGICAL punctuation: mark inside if it belongs to the quote, outside if it belongs to the outer sentence. American style just always tucks them inside. Source: Fowler's Modern English Usage.

question: 'She whispered "come here" then she vanished.' A semicolon is needed between the two independent clauses. Where does it go relative to the closing quotation mark?
answer: Outside the closing quotation mark: 'She whispered "come here"; then she vanished.'
choices: Outside the closing quotation mark: 'She whispered "come here"; then she vanished.'
Inside the closing quotation mark: 'She whispered "come here;" then she vanished.'
Both inside AND outside: 'She whispered "come here;"; then she vanished.'
context: Colons and semicolons ALWAYS go outside the closing quotation mark in BOTH American and British styles -- no exceptions. Only the period-and-comma rule differs. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.10.

question: Compare: (1) 'She asked, "Are you coming?"' (question mark inside) vs (2) 'Did she say "come here"?' (question mark outside). What determines which style is right?
answer: Whose question it is -- inside if the QUOTED material is the question; outside if the WHOLE sentence is the question about the quote
choices: Whose question it is -- inside if the QUOTED material is the question; outside if the WHOLE sentence is the question about the quote
American style always puts it inside; British always outside -- like periods
It is always outside in modern usage
It is always inside in modern usage
context: For question marks and exclamation points, both American and British follow logic. Only periods and commas are treated differently across the Atlantic. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.70.

question: A technical-writing manual quotes a computer command: 'Type "help", then press Enter.' It puts the comma OUTSIDE the closing quotation mark, matching BRITISH style. Why does an American technical writer sometimes do this?
answer: Precision in quoting code: putting the comma inside would suggest it is part of the command
choices: Precision in quoting code: putting the comma inside would suggest it is part of the command
British style is universally required for computer books
American house style now agrees with British on all punctuation
It is always an error -- American style should be followed
context: In technical contexts (quoting commands, code, filenames), some American style guides adopt British-style logical punctuation to avoid inserting extra characters into strings. Domain-specific exception; not a general rule. Source: Linguistic Society of America style guide.

question: Under standard AMERICAN style, which of these sentences correctly punctuates the quoted material?
answer: 'She said, "hello," then waved goodbye.'
choices: 'She said "hello"; then waved goodbye.' with the comma missing
context: American rule: comma INSIDE the closing quotation mark. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.9.

question: A friend tells you 'I need to stop by the ATM machine.' If you expand ATM to what it stands for, what does she just say?
answer: Automatic Teller Machine machine
context: ATM = Automatic Teller Machine. So 'ATM machine' says 'machine' twice. It is the canonical example of a redundant acronym. Source: Grokipedia 'RAS syndrome' (2026-09-05).

question: Your dad says 'Don't forget your PIN when you use the card.' PIN stands for Personal Identification ___. If you also say 'PIN ___,' you are repeating the last word twice. What word fills both blanks?
answer: Number
context: PIN = Personal Identification Number. So 'PIN number' expands to 'Personal Identification Number number.' Same trap: VIN = Vehicle Identification Number. Source: Grokipedia 'RAS syndrome' (2026-09-05).

question: In writing, REDUNDANCY means using two or more words that carry the same meaning, so one repeats the other and adds length without adding information. Which phrase is redundant in that sense?
answer: advance planning
context: Planning is by definition done in advance -- so 'advance planning' says 'planning planning.' The other three narrow the KIND of planning (careful, long-term, family). Source: Fowler's Modern English Usage, entry 'redundancy, tautology'.

question: A greeting card promises 'A FREE GIFT with every purchase!' Which word makes the phrase redundant?
answer: free -- a gift is by definition free
choices: free -- a gift is by definition free
context: Gifts are already given without payment; 'free gift' says 'free' twice. Standard redundancies of this shape: END RESULT (results come at the end), CLOSE PROXIMITY (proximity means closeness). Source: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage, entry 'redundancy'.

question: Standard redundant phrases repeat a word already implied by another. Which of these is NOT redundant?
answer: the tallest building in the city
choices: the tallest building in the city
context: History is by definition past; plans by definition point to the future; results come at the end. But 'tallest building in the city' just names a real superlative -- nothing repeats. Source: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage, entry 'redundancy'.

question: A doctor writes about 'the HIV virus' in a medical brochure. HIV stands for Human Immunodeficiency Virus. What is the meta-joke name for this whole category of redundancy?
answer: RAS syndrome -- Redundant Acronym Syndrome syndrome
choices: RAS syndrome -- Redundant Acronym Syndrome syndrome
context: 'RAS syndrome' itself is a self-example: Redundant Acronym Syndrome syndrome. Same trap: LCD DISPLAY = Liquid Crystal Display display; PIN NUMBER = Personal Identification Number number. Source: Grokipedia 'RAS syndrome' (2026-09-05).

question: A morning-radio host reads a promo: 'Join us at seven a.m. in the morning for my personal opinion on last night's game.' Which part is REDUNDANT?
answer: 'seven a.m. in the morning' AND 'my personal opinion' are both redundant
choices: 'seven a.m. in the morning' AND 'my personal opinion' are both redundant
only 'seven a.m. in the morning' is redundant
context: 'a.m.' already means morning; opinions are already personal. 'Last night's game' just names a specific game -- nothing repeats. Source: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage, entry 'redundancy'.

question: 'She saw ___ in the mirror.' Which reflexive pronoun?
answer: herself (subject and object are the same person)
choices: herself (subject and object are the same person)
context: REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) are used when the subject and object of a verb refer to the SAME person or thing.

question: 'The teacher gave the awards to my friend and myself.' What is wrong with 'myself' here?
answer: 'myself' needs an antecedent 'I' in the same sentence; use 'me'
choices: 'myself' needs an antecedent 'I' in the same sentence; use 'me'
context: REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS point back to a subject in the same sentence. 'I hurt myself' (I is the antecedent). Using 'myself' as a fancy 'me' with no 'I' is a hypercorrection. Chicago 5.51.

question: 'Between you and myself, this is a bad idea.' What is the correction?
answer: 'between you and me' -- object of preposition; no reflexive needed
choices: 'between you and me' -- object of preposition; no reflexive needed
context: Prepositions take object pronouns. 'Myself' has no antecedent 'I' in the sentence, so it cannot be reflexive. Use plain 'me'. Same hypercorrection as 'between you and I'.

question: Which reflexive-pronoun use is CORRECT?
answer: I hurt myself while running.
choices: Please send your report to Sarah or myself.
The gift is from Bob and myself.
The manager and myself will attend.
context: 'I hurt myself' -- subject 'I' matches reflexive 'myself'. The other three use 'myself' with no 'I' subject; they are hypercorrections for plain 'me' or 'I'.

question: The two legitimate uses of reflexive pronouns are ___.
answer: referring back to a subject in the same clause, OR emphasising a noun ('the president himself called')
choices: referring back to a subject in the same clause, OR emphasising a noun ('the president himself called')
context: REFLEXIVE use: subject and object are the same ('she washed herself'). INTENSIVE use: emphasises a noun ('I myself will attend'). Third-party fancy-me substitution is the hypercorrection to avoid.

question: 'The manager and myself will attend.' What is the correction?
answer: 'the manager and I' -- subject of the verb 'will attend'
choices: 'the manager and I' -- subject of the verb 'will attend'
context: Compound subject: use subject pronouns (I, not me or myself). Drop test: 'I will attend' (correct); 'me will attend' (wrong); 'myself will attend' (also wrong -- no antecedent).

question: 'The chef prepared the meal himself.' What role does 'himself' play here?
answer: intensive (emphasises that the chef, not a helper, did it)
choices: intensive (emphasises that the chef, not a helper, did it)
context: INTENSIVE use of reflexive pronouns emphasises a noun or pronoun. 'The chef himself' = 'the chef, not anyone else'. Removable without breaking grammar: 'The chef prepared the meal' is still complete.

question: Which sentence uses 'myself' correctly?
answer: I taught myself to code.
choices: The letter was addressed to my colleague and myself.
My colleague and myself will speak at the meeting.
Please forward the invoice to myself directly.
context: Only the first has 'I' as the subject with 'myself' as the object. The others use 'myself' as a fancy 'me' or 'I' with no antecedent -- hypercorrections in each case.

question: In English, REGISTER means the level of formality a writer or speaker chooses to fit the audience and occasion -- a text to a friend is written differently from a job application. Which of these would MOST need a formal register?
answer: A cover letter to a hiring manager
choices: A cover letter to a hiring manager
A birthday card to a sister
A note stuck on the fridge
context: Cover letters go to strangers with hiring power -- they need full words, no slang, courteous distance. The other three are for close family or the household. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: 'Hey, wanna grab lunch?' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Casual
context: Contractions ('wanna'), slang ('grab'), short, informal address ('hey') -- the mark of the casual register used in texts and chats between friends. Source: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage, entry 'register'.

question: 'Dear Ms. Smith, I would like to inquire about the position advertised on Monday.' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Formal
context: Full words (no contractions), courteous distance ('Dear Ms. Smith'), no slang. Used in business letters, job applications, formal invitations. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: 'This paper examines the relationship between sleep and short-term memory in seventh-graders.' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Academic
context: Third-person voice, precise vocabulary, a signal that sources will be cited. That is the essay-and-research-paper register. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: 'The compiler flags a segmentation fault at line 47.' Which register does that sentence use?
answer: Technical
context: 'Compiler,' 'segmentation fault,' 'line 47' -- specialized vocabulary for a specific field (programming). Technical register is used in manuals, specifications, and engineering documents. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: Carl Sandburg opened a short poem in 1916 with 'The fog comes on little cat feet.' Which register uses inventive vocabulary, figurative language, rhythm, and imagery like that?
answer: Literary
context: The comparison of fog to a cat is imagery, not report. Sandburg's 'Fog' (1916) is the classroom-standard example of the literary register. Source: Grokipedia 'Register (sociolinguistics)' (2026-09-05).

question: A student writes an essay opening: 'So basically what this paper's gonna be about is how kids sleep matters a bunch for memory and stuff.' If the assignment calls for the ACADEMIC register, what is the main problem?
answer: The register is CASUAL -- contractions and slang do not fit an academic essay
choices: The register is CASUAL -- contractions and slang do not fit an academic essay
The subject is wrong -- essays cannot discuss sleep
The tense is wrong -- academic essays must use past tense
The length is wrong -- essay openings must fill at least half a page
context: 'Basically,' 'gonna,' 'kids,' 'a bunch,' 'and stuff' are the casual register. An academic essay needs precise vocabulary and third-person voice. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.220.

question: 'She is one of the students who ___ hard.' Which verb form?
answer: work (WHO refers to 'students', a plural)
context: The relative-clause agreement rule: the verb inside the relative clause agrees with the noun the relative pronoun refers to. 'Who' → 'students' (plural) → 'work'. Chicago 5.66.

question: 'She is the only one of the students who ___ hard.' Now which verb?
answer: works (WHO now refers to 'one'; ONLY ONE narrows to a singular)
choices: works (WHO now refers to 'one'; ONLY ONE narrows to a singular)
context: 'THE ONLY ONE' shifts the relative reference to 'one' (singular). Compare 'one of the students who work' (plural) vs 'the only one of the students who works' (singular). Chicago 5.66.

question: 'The book that ___ on the table is mine.' Which verb?
answer: is (THAT refers to 'book', singular)
context: The relative pronoun THAT refers to its antecedent BOOK (singular). Verb agrees with BOOK → 'is'. Not with any other noun in the sentence.

question: 'The list of items that ___ missing is long.' Which verb?
answer: are (THAT refers to 'items', plural)
context: 'That' refers to ITEMS (plural), so verb inside the relative clause is 'are'. The main clause verb 'is' agrees with LIST (singular). Two separate agreements in one sentence.

question: 'He is one of those people who ___ never late.' Which verb?
answer: are (WHO refers to 'people', plural)
context: The classic 'one of those...who' construction. WHO refers to PEOPLE (plural), so verb is plural. 'One of those runners who never quit'; 'one of those songs that stay in your head'.

question: Which sentence follows the relative-clause agreement rule correctly?
answer: She is one of the writers who work at night.
choices: She is one of the writers who work at night.
She is one of the writers who works at night.
She is one of the writers whom works at night.
She is one of the writers whose works at night.
context: WHO refers to 'writers' (plural) → 'work'. The 'one of the X who' construction takes plural verb because WHO refers to X. 'The only one of the writers who works' would be singular.

question: 'A pile of books that ___ falling over sat in the corner.' Which verb?
answer: were (THAT refers to 'books', plural)
context: 'That' inside the relative clause refers to BOOKS (plural) → 'were falling'. The main clause verb 'sat' has 'pile' (singular) as subject. Two verbs, two different agreements.

question: 'The dog that bit me ran off' has no commas. 'The dog, which bit me, ran off' has commas. What is the DIFFERENCE these two sentences send to the reader?
answer: The no-comma version tells you WHICH dog (essential info); the comma version adds extra info about the one dog we already know
choices: The no-comma version tells you WHICH dog (essential info); the comma version adds extra info about the one dog we already know
The comma version means the dog was fake
The no-comma version is always past tense; the comma version is always present
The two versions mean exactly the same thing
context: Essential-to-identify = RESTRICTIVE (no commas, often THAT). Added-info = NON-RESTRICTIVE (commas, WHICH in American usage). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.27.

question: A friend says 'The dog, which bit me, ran off.' Based on the commas, how many dogs are we talking about?
answer: One dog -- the info is added, not identifying
choices: One dog -- the info is added, not identifying
Many dogs -- the commas identify which one
Two dogs -- one bit, one ran
It cannot be determined from the sentence
context: Commas mark non-restrictive (added info) -- the dog was already identifiable; the biting is added detail. Without commas the sentence would imply multiple dogs and pick out the biter. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.27.

question: In American formal writing, which punctuation is preferred for a RESTRICTIVE clause (essential to identifying which one)?
answer: 'The book that I read yesterday was great.' -- THAT, no commas
choices: 'The book that I read yesterday was great.' -- THAT, no commas
'The book, which I read yesterday, was great.' -- WHICH, with commas
'The book which I read yesterday was great.' -- WHICH, no commas
'The book, that I read yesterday was great.' -- THAT, one comma
context: American style (Chicago, AP) reserves THAT for restrictive and WHICH-with-commas for non-restrictive. British usage often uses WHICH for both. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.27.

question: 'Chicago ___ sits on Lake Michigan ___ has cold winters.' How should this be punctuated?
answer: 'Chicago, which sits on Lake Michigan, has cold winters.' -- commas around WHICH clause
choices: 'Chicago, which sits on Lake Michigan, has cold winters.' -- commas around WHICH clause
'Chicago that sits on Lake Michigan has cold winters.' -- no commas, THAT
'Chicago which sits on Lake Michigan has cold winters.' -- no commas, WHICH
'Chicago; which sits on Lake Michigan; has cold winters.' -- semicolons
context: Chicago is a unique proper noun; the clause cannot RESTRICT it, only add info. Non-restrictive clauses with a unique noun always take commas and WHICH (in American usage). Source: Grokipedia 'English relative clauses' (2026-09-05).

question: A British newspaper prints 'The train which arrived at platform three was delayed.' Under which house style is this sentence written?
answer: British -- WHICH is used for restrictive AND non-restrictive clauses; American style would use THAT here
choices: British -- WHICH is used for restrictive AND non-restrictive clauses; American style would use THAT here
American -- WHICH is required for all clauses
Chicago Manual -- the standard for all English
Academic -- all essays must use WHICH
context: No commas mean the clause is restrictive (which train). British writers accept WHICH here; American style guides would use THAT. Source: Fowler's 'Modern English Usage' on that/which.

question: 'The students who studied passed the test.' vs 'The students, who studied, passed the test.' What is the meaning difference the commas create?
answer: No commas: only the students who studied passed. With commas: all the students studied, and all of them passed.
choices: No commas: only the students who studied passed. With commas: all the students studied, and all of them passed.
No commas: the students were rewarded. With commas: they were punished.
The two versions mean exactly the same thing.
The comma version is grammatically wrong.
context: Restrictive (no commas) filters -- 'the students who studied' is a subset. Non-restrictive (commas) adds info about ALL the students. Same sentence, two different worlds. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.27.

question: Which of these sentences is punctuated CORRECTLY in American style?
answer: 'The car that I bought last week already has a flat tire.'
choices: 'The car that I bought last week already has a flat tire.'
'The car, that I bought last week, already has a flat tire.'
'The car which I bought last week already has a flat tire.'
'The car; which I bought last week; already has a flat tire.'
context: Restrictive clause (identifies WHICH car): THAT, no commas. Non-restrictive with unique reference would take commas and WHICH. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.27.

question: 'The rain fell birds took shelter.' What error is this?
answer: run-on (fused) sentence -- two full sentences with no punctuation between them
choices: run-on (fused) sentence -- two full sentences with no punctuation between them
context: RUN-ON (fused) SENTENCE: two independent clauses smashed together with NO punctuation or conjunction. Compare comma splice (has a comma). Both errors, run-on is worse. Chicago 5.219.

question: Which fix is NOT valid for a run-on sentence?
answer: leave it alone -- run-ons are stylistic choices
choices: leave it alone -- run-ons are stylistic choices
context: RUN-ONS are always errors in standard English. Standard fixes: (1) period, (2) semicolon, (3) comma + FANBOYS, (4) subordinate one clause. Stylistic run-ons in fiction ('stream of consciousness') are a separate rare exception.

question: 'She wrote the letter she mailed it.' Best fix?
answer: 'She wrote the letter. She mailed it.' OR 'She wrote the letter, and she mailed it.'
choices: 'She wrote the letter. She mailed it.' OR 'She wrote the letter, and she mailed it.'
'She wrote the letter she mailed it,'
context: Standard run-on fixes: period between clauses, or comma + coordinating conjunction. Either works. Semicolon also works: 'She wrote the letter; she mailed it.'

question: Difference between COMMA SPLICE and RUN-ON (fused) sentence?
answer: splice has a comma between clauses; run-on has no punctuation at all
choices: splice has a comma between clauses; run-on has no punctuation at all
run-on is a comma splice with two commas
context: COMMA SPLICE = comma between full clauses ('It rained, we left'). FUSED / RUN-ON = no punctuation ('It rained we left'). Same error family, different severity.

question: 'The clock struck midnight everyone cheered.' Which fix keeps the two events feeling tightly linked?
answer: semicolon: 'The clock struck midnight; everyone cheered.'
choices: semicolon: 'The clock struck midnight; everyone cheered.'
context: SEMICOLON is the tightest of the standard fixes -- signals a strong link between related events. Period feels more separated. Both are valid run-on fixes; choose based on desired connection.

question: Which sentence is a run-on?
answer: The dog barked the mailman ran.
choices: The dog barked the mailman ran.
The dog barked, and the mailman ran.
The dog barked; the mailman ran.
The dog barked. The mailman ran.
context: First option: no punctuation between two full sentences = fused (run-on). The other three all use one of the standard fixes: comma + conjunction, semicolon, period.

question: 'It was cold I put on a jacket then I went outside.' How many independent clauses are running on?
answer: three (it was cold / I put on a jacket / I went outside)
choices: three (it was cold / I put on a jacket / I went outside)
context: Each independent clause could be its own sentence: 'It was cold.' 'I put on a jacket.' 'I went outside.' All fused together = run-on. Fix: three sentences, or use punctuation between each.

question: A user manual: "ONE SHOULD TAKE THE BOX AND CARRY IT TO THE KITCHEN." Why does this read stiff?
answer: it uses THIRD-PERSON when the imperative ("Take the box to the kitchen") would be direct
choices: it uses THIRD-PERSON when the imperative ("Take the box to the kitchen") would be direct
context: Instructions want the IMPERATIVE (YOU understood). "One should" adds distance and stiffness.

question: What is the IMPERATIVE mood?
answer: a verb form that gives a command; the subject "you" is usually understood
choices: a verb form that gives a command; the subject "you" is usually understood
a verb form that describes a past event
a verb form that asks a question
a verb form that expresses a wish
context: IMPERATIVE = command mood. "Close the door" means "YOU close the door" -- YOU is dropped.

question: Which sentence is written in the IMPERATIVE mood?
answer: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees
choices: One should preheat the oven to 350 degrees
The oven should be preheated to 350 degrees
context: IMPERATIVE = direct command with YOU understood. The others use third person, passive, or gerund.

question: A recipe reads "combine the flour and the sugar" vs "one should combine the flour and the sugar." Why does the imperative win?
answer: it reads like a friend at your elbow; the third-person adds unnecessary distance
choices: it reads like a friend at your elbow; the third-person adds unnecessary distance
context: Instructional writing wants immediacy. The imperative is direct, friendly, and clear.

question: Which register sometimes AVOIDS imperatives?
answer: formal academic and legal writing ("the applicant should complete section 3")
choices: formal academic and legal writing ("the applicant should complete section 3")
context: Formal legal/academic registers sometimes soften with third-person and modal verbs. Everyday instructions use imperatives.

question: Which is the BEST instructional form for "getting the box to the kitchen"?
answer: Take the box to the kitchen
choices: Take the box to the kitchen
One should take the box to the kitchen
The box should be taken to the kitchen
Taking the box to the kitchen is necessary
context: IMPERATIVE = direct and clear for instructions. The others are stiff third-person, passive, or noun-phrased.

question: In Middle English around the year 1300, the word NICE actually meant something close to the OPPOSITE of its modern sense. The Middle-English meaning came from Latin 'nescius' -- 'not knowing.' What did NICE mean back then?
answer: Foolish, silly, or ignorant
context: Over roughly six centuries NICE drifted: foolish -> shy -> refined -> kind. That kind of change is called SEMANTIC SHIFT. Source: OED 'nice.'

question: In the 1500s, God was described as AWFUL. That was a wholly POSITIVE thing to say. What did AWFUL mean then?
answer: Full of awe -- awe-inspiring, majestic
context: AWFUL = 'full of awe.' Today the meaning has flipped -- AWFUL means bad, and AWESOME took over the positive sense. Source: OED 'awful.'

question: In Old English (around the year 900) the word SILLY -- spelled 'saelig' -- meant something quite different from today. What did it mean?
answer: Blessed, happy, holy
context: SILLY shares a root with German 'selig' (blessed). Over centuries it drifted: blessed -> innocent -> defenseless -> foolish (by ~1600). Source: OED 'silly.'

question: In Middle English around 1300, the word GIRL had a broader meaning than today -- broad enough that a boy could be called one. What did GIRL mean back then?
answer: A young person of either sex
choices: A young person of either sex
A blood relative in one's own household
context: GIRL narrowed to 'young female' by the 1500s. Bill Bryson uses this in 'Mother Tongue' (1990) as a favorite example of semantic NARROWING -- a word whose meaning shrinks. Source: OED 'girl'; Bryson (1990).

question: MEAT in Old English meant 'any food' -- bread was meat, apples were meat. Today MEAT means only flesh food. Which category of semantic shift is this?
answer: Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
choices: Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
Pejoration -- the meaning became more negative
context: Any-food -> flesh-only is a smaller set: narrowing. Same shape: GIRL (any young person -> young female). Source: Grokipedia 'Semantic change' (2026-09-05).

question: In Old English a KNIGHT (cniht) was simply a boy or a young male servant. Today a KNIGHT is a noble warrior with lands and a title. Which category of semantic shift is this?
answer: Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
choices: Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
Pejoration -- the meaning became more negative
Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
context: Boy-servant -> noble warrior is a step up in status: amelioration. The mirror pattern is PEJORATION: VILLAIN was once just a farm worker (villein); now it means criminal. Source: Grokipedia 'Semantic change' (2026-09-05).

question: HOLIDAY comes from HOLY DAY. Once only religious feasts were holidays; now any day off from work or school counts. Which category of semantic shift is this?
answer: Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
choices: Widening -- the meaning grew to a larger set
Narrowing -- the meaning shrank to a smaller set
Amelioration -- the meaning became more positive
Pejoration -- the meaning became more negative
context: Holy-day-only -> any-day-off is a bigger set: widening. Same shape: DOG was originally a specific breed name; now it covers all dogs. Source: Grokipedia 'Semantic change' (2026-09-05).

question: 'I have lived in Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.' Why are those SEMICOLONS between the city-country pairs instead of just commas?
answer: Because each item already contains a comma; semicolons serve as super-commas to keep items distinct
choices: Because each item already contains a comma; semicolons serve as super-commas to keep items distinct
Because semicolons are more formal than commas
Because the list has exactly three items
Because English lists always use semicolons
context: When list items themselves contain commas, ordinary comma-separation blurs the boundaries. Semicolons step up as super-commas. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: 'I have lived in Paris, France, Rome, Italy, and Athens, Greece.' Why is this comma-only version broken?
answer: The reader cannot tell if 'France, Rome' is one item or two -- semicolons between items would fix it
choices: The reader cannot tell if 'France, Rome' is one item or two -- semicolons between items would fix it
It has too many capital letters
It is missing an Oxford comma
The word AND should not appear before the final item
context: Ambiguity of item boundaries is exactly what super-commas solve. Rewrite as 'Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.' Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: Which of these lists correctly uses SUPER-COMMAS (semicolons) between items with internal commas?
answer: 'Deadlines are July 4, 1776; December 7, 1941; and September 11, 2001.'
context: Dates contain commas (July 4, 1776). Using commas between them too would blur the boundaries. Semicolons keep the three deadlines distinct. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: 'The speakers were Dr. Alice Chen our chief scientist Mr. Ben Ortiz the operations director and Prof. Carla Vega the department head.' What is the cleanest fix?
answer: Add appositive commas and use SEMICOLONS between speakers: 'Dr. Alice Chen, our chief scientist; Mr. Ben Ortiz, the operations director; and Prof. Carla Vega, the department head.'
choices: Add appositive commas and use SEMICOLONS between speakers: 'Dr. Alice Chen, our chief scientist; Mr. Ben Ortiz, the operations director; and Prof. Carla Vega, the department head.'
Add only commas everywhere -- more commas mean more clarity
Add colons between speakers -- colons always separate list items
Add periods between speakers -- treat each as a separate sentence
context: Each speaker's name is followed by an appositive (with commas), so semicolons between speakers keep the three people distinct. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: 'She invited her sister Anna her brother Ben and her mother Carla' -- a light-comma list where each item has a single appositive. What does Chicago recommend for clarity?
answer: Use semicolons between items even here: 'her sister, Anna; her brother, Ben; and her mother, Carla' -- prefer super-commas whenever items carry internal commas
choices: Use semicolons between items even here: 'her sister, Anna; her brother, Ben; and her mother, Carla' -- prefer super-commas whenever items carry internal commas
Never use semicolons in personal-relationship lists
Use only commas -- semicolons are pretentious
Rewrite the sentence to avoid the problem entirely
context: Even in a light case, Chicago prefers semicolons when items carry appositive commas -- the reader sees the item boundaries clearly. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.60.

question: 'It was late; however, we kept working.' Two independent clauses joined by HOWEVER. What punctuation does HOWEVER need before and after it?
answer: Semicolon BEFORE and comma AFTER: '; however,'
choices: Semicolon BEFORE and comma AFTER: '; however,'
Comma BEFORE and comma AFTER: ', however,'
Semicolon BEFORE and semicolon AFTER: '; however;'
context: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover) joining two independent clauses need a SEMICOLON before and a COMMA after. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: 'It was late, however we kept working.' This is called a comma splice. Which fix is right?
answer: Replace the comma with a semicolon and add a comma after HOWEVER: 'It was late; however, we kept working.'
choices: Replace the comma with a semicolon and add a comma after HOWEVER: 'It was late; however, we kept working.'
Add BUT before HOWEVER: 'It was late, but however we kept working.'
The sentence is fine as written -- HOWEVER can follow a comma
context: HOWEVER is a conjunctive adverb, not a FANBOYS. A comma alone before it creates a comma splice between two independent clauses. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: 'It was late. However we kept working.' When HOWEVER starts a NEW sentence (after a period), what punctuation does it take?
answer: Just a comma AFTER: 'However, we kept working.'
choices: Just a comma AFTER: 'However, we kept working.'
A semicolon BEFORE and comma AFTER: '; However, we kept working.'
No punctuation -- it starts a sentence clean
A colon AFTER: 'However: we kept working.'
context: There is a period before, so no semicolon is needed. The sentence-initial conjunctive adverb takes only the comma after. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: Three families of connective words take different punctuation. Which of these correctly describes the split?
answer: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore) take a semicolon before + comma after; FANBOYS coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) take a comma before; subordinating conjunctions (because, although) take a comma only when the dependent clause LEADS
choices: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore) take a semicolon before + comma after; FANBOYS coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) take a comma before; subordinating conjunctions (because, although) take a comma only when the dependent clause LEADS
All three families take the same punctuation (a comma before)
Conjunctive adverbs and FANBOYS both take a semicolon; only subordinating conjunctions differ
Only conjunctive adverbs take any punctuation; FANBOYS and subordinating conjunctions take none
context: Three families, three punctuation patterns. Mixing them up is one of the most common formal-writing errors. Source: Grokipedia 'Conjunctive adverb' (2026-09-05).

question: 'We, however, kept working through the night.' Why does this sentence take commas around HOWEVER rather than a semicolon before?
answer: HOWEVER is a MID-CLAUSE parenthetical adverb here, interrupting one clause -- commas set it off on both sides
choices: HOWEVER is a MID-CLAUSE parenthetical adverb here, interrupting one clause -- commas set it off on both sides
The sentence starts with WE -- HOWEVER never takes a semicolon after a pronoun
The sentence is a fragment -- semicolons need two independent clauses
HOWEVER always takes commas, never semicolons
context: The semicolon-before pattern is only for HOWEVER joining TWO independent clauses. Inside one clause, HOWEVER is just a parenthetical adverb, set off by commas. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: Which of these sentences correctly punctuates the conjunctive adverb THEREFORE joining two independent clauses?
answer: 'The road was blocked; therefore, we took the long way home.'
choices: 'The road was blocked; therefore, we took the long way home.'
'The road was blocked, therefore we took the long way home.'
'The road was blocked, therefore, we took the long way home.'
'The road was blocked therefore we took the long way home.'
context: THEREFORE, like HOWEVER, is a conjunctive adverb. Semicolon before + comma after joins two independent clauses. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 6.57.

question: 'The rain stopped; the sun came out.' What is the semicolon's job here?
answer: joining two independent clauses closely related in meaning
choices: joining two independent clauses closely related in meaning
showing a pause longer than a comma
context: The semicolon's primary job: joining two independent clauses (each could be its own sentence) that are closely related. Chicago 6.56.

question: 'She loves reading; her sister prefers movies.' Why not use a comma here instead?
answer: a comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice
choices: a comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice
context: Two independent clauses joined by comma alone = comma splice (a punctuation error). Fixes: semicolon, period, or add a coordinating conjunction (comma + and/but/or).

question: 'She packed her bag; and left for the airport.' What is wrong with this semicolon?
answer: semicolons do not take a following coordinating conjunction like 'and'
choices: semicolons do not take a following coordinating conjunction like 'and'
context: The semicolon already does the joining -- 'and' becomes redundant. Use EITHER a semicolon OR a comma+conjunction, not both.

question: 'I have visited three cities: Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.' Why semicolons in the list instead of commas?
answer: the list items themselves contain commas; semicolons act as super-commas
choices: the list items themselves contain commas; semicolons act as super-commas
cities are always separated by semicolons
the list is too long for commas
context: When list items already contain commas (Paris, France), commas as separators create ambiguity. Semicolons serve as super-commas to keep items distinct. Chicago 6.58.

question: 'The meeting was short; however, the decisions were huge.' What role does the semicolon play with the word 'however'?
answer: joins two independent clauses; 'however' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction
choices: joins two independent clauses; 'however' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction
shows a pause before the however
cancels the meaning of the first clause
context: 'However', 'therefore', 'moreover', 'nevertheless' are conjunctive adverbs. They CANNOT join clauses grammatically -- you need a semicolon (or a period) before them, and a comma after. Chicago 6.57.

question: 'The path was steep; and rocky and slippery.' What is the correct fix?
answer: drop the semicolon: 'The path was steep and rocky and slippery' (one clause)
choices: drop the semicolon: 'The path was steep and rocky and slippery' (one clause)
context: 'And rocky and slippery' is NOT an independent clause -- it's a list of predicate adjectives. Semicolons only join independent clauses; if only one side has a subject and verb, no semicolon.

question: 'She wrote the letter; because she felt she owed him a reply.' What is wrong?
answer: 'because...' is a dependent clause; semicolons only join independent clauses
choices: 'because...' is a dependent clause; semicolons only join independent clauses
context: 'Because she felt she owed him a reply' cannot stand alone (starts with subordinating conjunction 'because'). Semicolons join TWO INDEPENDENT clauses. Fix: 'She wrote the letter because she felt...' (no punctuation).

question: 'Ran quickly down the street.' What is missing?
answer: the subject (WHO ran?)
context: SENTENCE FRAGMENT (missing subject): a group of words with a verb but no subject cannot stand alone as a sentence. Fix by adding a subject: 'She ran quickly down the street.'

question: 'Sat on the bench for hours.' What kind of fragment is this?
answer: missing-subject fragment (no one is doing the sitting)
choices: missing-subject fragment (no one is doing the sitting)
context: The verb 'sat' has no subject. Who or what sat? Fix by adding a subject: 'He sat on the bench for hours.' or 'The old cat sat on the bench for hours.'

question: Which sentence is a fragment because of a missing subject?
answer: Walked into the room silently.
choices: The tall woman walked into the room silently.
context: 'Walked into the room silently' has no subject. Who walked? The others either have a subject (the tall woman) or are participial phrases (which are also fragments but for a different reason).

question: 'Was tired after the long day.' Fix.
answer: 'She was tired after the long day.' (add subject)
choices: 'She was tired after the long day.' (add subject)
context: 'Was tired' has no subject. WHO was tired? Fix by adding one: 'She was tired' or 'The runner was tired'. Every English sentence needs a subject (imperatives have an implied 'you').

question: 'Painted the entire room in one afternoon.' Which subject would fix the fragment?
answer: 'She painted the entire room in one afternoon.'
choices: 'She painted the entire room in one afternoon.'
context: Add a subject to the verb 'painted' to complete the sentence. Almost any noun/pronoun that could paint (she, he, the crew, my father) works.

question: Why do missing-subject fragments happen frequently in writing?
answer: writers omit subjects that seem obvious from context, but each sentence needs its own subject
choices: writers omit subjects that seem obvious from context, but each sentence needs its own subject
context: In speech and casual writing, we drop subjects when context is clear ('Sat there for hours.'). Formal writing requires each sentence to have its own explicit subject.

question: 'Went to the store yesterday. Bought bread and milk. Came home tired.' What is the issue?
answer: three fragments in a row -- each sentence lacks a subject
choices: three fragments in a row -- each sentence lacks a subject
context: The passage reads casually, but each sentence lacks a subject. Fix: 'I went to the store yesterday. I bought bread and milk. I came home tired.' Common in speech; problematic in formal writing.

question: 'The huge orange cat on the windowsill.' You keep reading and there is nothing more. What is wrong with this as a complete sentence?
answer: It is a fragment -- no verb; the cat never does anything
choices: It is a fragment -- no verb; the cat never does anything
It has too many adjectives -- cats can only have one color
It has a comma error -- there should be a comma after CAT
It is a run-on -- two ideas jammed together
context: Every sentence needs at least a subject + verb pair. Here the subject (cat) sits alone with no verb (sat, watched, slept, jumped). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.213.

question: A noun phrase names a person, place, or thing but has no verb to tell you what it does. That kind of standalone piece is called what?
answer: A sentence fragment
context: A FRAGMENT is a piece missing something it needs -- most often a verb, sometimes a subject. Source: Grokipedia 'Sentence clause structure' (2026-09-05).

question: Which of these is a FRAGMENT (not a complete sentence)?
answer: 'My grandmother's amazing chocolate chip cookies with walnuts.'
choices: 'My grandmother's amazing chocolate chip cookies with walnuts.'
context: The first option is only a subject (a big noun phrase) with no verb -- fragment. The other three each have a subject + a verb (are, baked, smell). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.213.

question: 'The huge orange cat on the windowsill.' Which fix turns this fragment into a complete sentence?
answer: 'The huge orange cat sat on the windowsill.'
choices: 'The huge orange cat sat on the windowsill.'
'The huge orange cat, on the windowsill.'
'The huge orange cat: on the windowsill.'
'The huge orange cat -- on the windowsill.'
context: Adding the verb SAT gives the subject something to do. Punctuation alone cannot fix a missing verb. Source: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage.

question: 'In the corner of the garage behind the old bicycles under a blue tarp.' Why is this a FRAGMENT even though it is long?
answer: It is a chain of prepositional phrases with no subject and no verb -- all setting, no action
choices: It is a chain of prepositional phrases with no subject and no verb -- all setting, no action
It is missing an Oxford comma
context: Every phrase starts with a preposition (in, of, behind, under). None of it acts as subject or verb. Fix: give it a subject and verb -- 'We found the puzzle in the corner of the garage.' Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.213.

question: A student writes: 'Because the storm knocked out the power.' Which fix turns this fragment into a complete sentence?
answer: 'Because the storm knocked out the power, we lit candles.'
choices: 'Because the storm knocked out the power, we lit candles.'
'Because the storm knocked out the power!'
'Because the storm, knocked out the power.'
'The, because, storm knocked out the power.'
context: 'Because the storm knocked out the power' is a SUBORDINATE clause. It has a subject (storm) and a verb (knocked out), but BECAUSE tells the reader the sentence must continue with a main clause. Only Option A adds a main clause ('we lit candles'). Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.213.

question: Which of these is a COMPLETE sentence (not a fragment)?
answer: 'The dog barked all night.'
choices: 'A very loud noise in the middle of the night.'
'Running down the hallway to the stairs.'
context: The first has subject (dog) + verb (barked). The others are: a noun phrase; a participial phrase; a subordinate clause. Each is a fragment on its own. Source: Chicago Manual of Style 17e section 5.213.

question: 'Because it was late.' Why is this a fragment?
answer: it is a subordinate clause with no independent clause to complete the thought
choices: it is a subordinate clause with no independent clause to complete the thought
